item.text: {"text":"NextItNet’s core design—causal dilated convolutions with residual identity shortcuts—supports learning across increasingly large history windows ([original paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.05163)). Relevant 2025–2026 work supports adaptive scale selection, although the search found no direct validation of the exact proposed NextItNet modification. [AD-TCN (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-00572-8) learns adaptive dilation factors and weights multi-scale features while retaining causal convolutions and residual connections; its experiments concern equipment lifetime prediction, so recommendation benefits remain unverified. [ScaleRec (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0306457325002596) distinguishes fine-grained interests from coarse-grained preferences through multiple temporal scales and context-adaptive aggregation, providing recommendation-specific motivation but using a Transformer backbone.\n\nA compatible research hypothesis is to replace the fixed recent-summary gate with input-dependent weights over several causal dilation branches inside each NextItNet residual block: h_out = h + Σ_s softmax(g(h))_s F_s(h). All branches and gates would train jointly within one model, preserving the identity shortcut and NextItNet backbone. Optionally condition gates on observed log-scaled inter-event gaps; earlier [time-aware recommendation research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598) demonstrates temporal gating for information filtering and state transitions, but does not establish this convolutional design. Elapsed time and interaction distance should remain distinct signals. Compare adaptive gates against the unchanged baseline and uniform scale weights using macro validation HR@10. These sources motivate testing context-dependent receptive fields; they do not establish that recent interactions should always dominate, or that deletion diagnostics identify causal importance."}
